intro: Formigine is a small town in the plain just south of Modena, and at its centre the neoclassical Villa Gandini stands in a public park, the Parco della Resistenza, with ponds, ducks and old trees. The two ginkgos on the villa's south side are the park's symbols, and each autumn they turn a clear gold over the water. A reader sent us their photographs.

trees.name: The Golden Ginkgos of Villa Gandini

location.address: Parco di Villa Gandini (Parco della Resistenza), south side of the villa, Formigine, Modena

trees.story:
"The two grand ginkgo bilobas on the south side of Villa Gandini are the symbols of the park," says Formigine's own tourism office, and in autumn a reader stood across the pond from them and sent us what they saw.

In their photographs the two crowns have turned the clear, even gold that only a ginkgo manages, so bright that the pale front of the villa looks grey beside them. The pond holds the whole scene upside down, ducks drifting through it, its surface scattered with small fan-shaped leaves already falling. Closer in, the reader shows one of the pair alone, its dark, short trunk under a crown so wide that its lowest limbs sweep down almost to the gravel, a bench in its shade and a wooden fence running along the water.

The reader puts the trees at 135 to 150 years old and one trunk at 457 centimetres round. Those figures are theirs; we have not seen them written down elsewhere, and we do not know who planted the pair.

A ginkgo tends to drop its leaves within days of turning, so the reader's "spectacular foliage in November" is a short show. Come then, and walk all the way round the pond.
trees.how_to_recognise: On the south side of the pale villa: two big ginkgos side by side beyond a pond with a small statue in it, a rail fence along the water, the nearer one a short dark trunk under a crown that sweeps almost to the gravel.

question_meta: The two golden ginkgos of Villa Gandini in Formigine, near Modena: where they stand in the park, when they turn, and what a reader told us.
question_answer: The Golden Ginkgos of Villa Gandini stand on the south side of the villa in Formigine's Parco della Resistenza, a public park open every day.
question_context: The two ginkgos on the south side of Villa Gandini are the symbols of the Parco della Resistenza in Formigine, a small town just south of Modena, according to the town's own tourism office. A reader sent us four photographs of them in autumn. In them the two crowns have turned the clear, even gold that only a ginkgo manages, so bright that the pale front of the villa looks grey beside them, and the pond in front of them holds the whole scene upside down, with ducks drifting across it and small fan-shaped leaves already on the water. One of the pair has a short dark trunk under a crown so wide that its lowest limbs sweep down almost to the gravel path, with a bench in its shade. The reader puts the trees at 135 to 150 years old and one trunk at 457 centimetres round; those figures are theirs. The park is public and open every day. Ginkgos tend to drop their leaves within days of turning, so November is the time to go.

faq.q: Can I visit The Golden Ginkgos of Villa Gandini?
faq.a: Yes. They stand in the public park around Villa Gandini in Formigine, which is free and open every day.

faq.q: When do the ginkgos of Villa Gandini turn gold?
faq.a: In autumn, usually in November, as in the reader's photographs. Ginkgos tend to drop their leaves within days of turning.

faq.q: How old are the ginkgos of Villa Gandini?
faq.a: A reader puts them at 135 to 150 years old. We have not found a written record of when they were planted.
